newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian lupins threatened by new disease.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian lupins threatened by new disease.

text.p: Australia's lupins industry has been placed under threat by the discovery for the first time in the country of a fungal disease in crops in Western Australia (WA).
The disease, anthracnose, has been discovered on four properties in Western Australia, the state farm department, Agriculture WA, said.
Australia has been one of the few countries in the world free of anthracnose.
Agriculture WA said it expected to issue a formal statement on the discovery of anthracnose soon.
A spokeswoman for the department later said anthracnose had now been confirmed on seven properties.
It was a little severe to say the disease posed the threat of wiping the lupin crop out, she said.
"It certainly has significant implications for the lupin industry," she said.
But different types of lupins had different susceptibility to the disease, she said.
Albus (white) lupins were most susceptible while narrow leaf lupin, the main industry, was least susceptible, she said.

The latest official forecast for 1996/97 - from the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) last week - put the state's lupins production at 765,000 tonnes out of a forecast national crop of 924,000 tonnes.
This was well down on the state's 1995/96 crop of 1.2 million tonnes out of a national crop of 1.43 million.
In its latest Crop Report, ABARE said fungal diseases had been a problem as far north as the Geraldton zone, particularly in albus crops on red loam soils.
"Agriculture WA is absolutely flat out working out eradication strategies," she said.
The way to combat the disease was to destroy affected crops. Departmental officials were working on eradication strategies this evening and were expected to make an announcement on Tuesday, she said.
Western Australia has long been Australia's leading lupin producing state.
The reduction in forecast national lupins production for 1996/97 reflected the lateness of the break to rain throughout most states, as well as relatively high cereal prices at the time of planting.
